code_label: Benchmarking parity transformation for QAOA
text_span: We present benchmarks of the parity trans- formation for the Quantum Approximate Op- timization Algorithm (QAOA).
rationale: States the paper's main objective.

code_label: Toy models of real-world scenarios
text_span: We analyse the gate resources required to implement a single QAOA cycle for toy models of real-world scenarios.
rationale: Defines the benchmark scope and evaluation target.

code_label: Three embedding strategies compared
text_span: We compare the number of gates required in three scenarios: a standard compiler using CNOT gates on a square lattice, the parity compiler on the same hardware with the same gates, and the parity compiler using parity gates (i.e. 4-body gates).
rationale: Specifies the comparative experimental setup.

code_label: Parity architecture reduces CNOT gates for spin models
text_span: For the spin models studied our ﬁndings imply a signiﬁcant advantage of the parity mapping compared to the standard gate model in terms of the number of CNOT gates required on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity, at the cost of an increased number of qubits.
rationale: Summarizes the main benchmark finding.

code_label: Potential to boost quantum advantage
text_span: Our results suggest that in combination with its full parallelizability of gates, the parity architecture has the potential to boost the race for demonstrating quantum advantage.
rationale: States an implication and forward-looking claim.

code_label: Need for hardware benchmarks
text_span: benchmarks of encoding of optimization problems on realistic hardware are a pressing need for the development of next generation quantum devices.
rationale: Motivates the benchmark study.

code_label: Parity mapping generalizes LHZ and supports higher-order constraints
text_span: The parity architecture [12], which generalizes the LHZ-architecture [13], allows one to implement problems with highly non-local higher-order terms, using only local interactions, and to encode constraints [14].
rationale: Describes the encoding approach being benchmarked.

code_label: Fully parallelizable gates
text_span: The LHZ-architecture, and to a large extent also the generalized parity scheme, can be implemented with fully parallelizable gates [15]
rationale: Highlights a hardware/circuit property relevant across the paper.

code_label: General Hamiltonian with arbitrary-order spin terms
text_span: Consider the general problem Hamiltonian for N qubits
rationale: Introduces the formal problem Hamiltonian used in the parity mapping.

code_label: Constraints preserve degrees of freedom
text_span: NC = K − N + D constraints have to be imposed in order to preserve the number of degrees of freedom, where D denotes the number of degeneracies in the original Hamilto- nian.
rationale: States a key mapping rule for the parity compiler.

code_label: Local plaquette constraints on square lattices
text_span: A constraint can be any product of k-body terms. However, for two-dimensional lattices, 3- and 4-body terms are the most practical, because it is crucial for implementations that constraints are geometrically local interactions, e.g. nearest neighbors on a square lattice.
rationale: Explains a design choice for implementable constraints.

code_label: QAOA uses alternating driver and problem unitaries
text_span: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [4] is a variational hybrid quantum-classical approach to tackle combinatorial optimization problems
rationale: Defines the algorithmic framework.

code_label: QAOA state preparation repeated p times
text_span: The integer p ≥ 1 is referred to as the QAOA depth or the number of QAOA cycles.
rationale: Identifies the repeated-cycle structure of the algorithm.

code_label: Parity QAOA splits problem unitary into local field and constraint parts
text_span: For QAOA in the parity scheme [15], the prob- lem Hamiltonian (2) can be split into the local ﬁeld part Hz = PK k=1 Jk˜σ(k) z and the constraint part HC = PNC l cl˜σ(l,1) z ˜σ(l,2) z ˜σ(l,3) z ˜σ(l,4) z .
rationale: Describes the parity-specific decomposition used in the protocol.

code_label: Parity QAOA adds extra parameter set
text_span: we obtain Uz(γ) = and Uc(Ω) =
rationale: Indicates the introduction of separate parameters for local fields and constraints.

code_label: Parity QAOA increases classical search space
text_span: This protocol enhances the ﬂexibility of the algorithm at the cost of enlarging the search space for the classical parameters.
rationale: States a tradeoff of the parity-QAOA formulation.

code_label: Standard gate model requires phase gadgets and SWAPs
text_span: As there might be non-local interactions in the problem Hamiltonian (i.e. interactions not neighboring on the square lattice), additional SWAP gates are required in the direct implementation.
locator: 3.1 QAOA in the standard gate model
rationale: Explains why the standard embedding can be costly.

code_label: Gate cost depends on interaction order and locality
text_span: the number of CNOT gates required for the implementation depends on (i) the number of terms in the problem Hamiltonian, (ii) their interaction order and (iii) the locality of the qubits involved in each inter- action.
locator: 3.1 QAOA in the standard gate model
rationale: Identifies the main drivers of resource use in the standard model.

code_label: Parity constraints avoid SWAP gates
text_span: As the constraints are local interactions, there is no need to use SWAP gates which makes the parity embed- ding highly parallelizable [15].
rationale: States a key implementation advantage of parity encoding.

code_label: Native 4-body couplers reduce gate count further
text_span: If the constraints can be implemented as single gate operations, the im- plementation in the standard gate model consumes (about) at least twice as many gates as the imple- mentation using the parity compiler
rationale: Summarizes the claimed gate-count advantage of native couplers.

code_label: Worst-case parity benchmark assumption
text_span: we assume the worst- case scenario for the parity mapping, namely that ev- ery constraint is a 4-body constraint and therefore consists of 6 CNOT gates.
rationale: States a conservative assumption used in benchmarking.

code_label: Parity CNOT upper bound
text_span: nPM CNOT = 6NC.
rationale: Defines the parity-model gate-count estimate.

code_label: Standard-model compilation uses t|ket⟩
text_span: For embedding QAOA in the standard gate model, we use the t|ket⟩ transpiler by Cambridge Quantum Computing (CQC) [32] to ﬁnd a good mapping of qubits on a square-lattice chip
rationale: Specifies the compiler used for the baseline comparison.

code_label: Gate ratio as figure of merit
text_span: Let us deﬁne the gate ratio rgates = nCNOT(PM) nCNOT(GM)
rationale: Defines the main comparison metric.

code_label: Linear growth of CNOTs with interaction count
text_span: We observe that the number of required CNOT gates grows linearly with K.
rationale: Reports a central empirical trend.

code_label: Higher-order interactions increase slope
text_span: the slope of the linear ﬁt grows with increasing k.
rationale: Shows that interaction order affects resource growth.

code_label: Parity advantage grows with system size and higher-order terms
text_span: These ﬁnding imply that the parity embedding shows a greater ad- vantage (i) for larger logical system sizes and (ii) if more high-order terms (order k > 2) are in- volved in the problem.
rationale: Summarizes the benchmark interpretation.

code_label: Average interaction order correlates with parity advantage
text_span: We observe that with a higher average interaction order the advantage of the parity architecture is more prominent.
rationale: Reports a second empirical trend from the mixed k-body graphs.

code_label: Caution about comparing different system sizes
text_span: this ﬁnding must be han- dled with care when only relying on that ﬁgure
rationale: Explicit caveat about interpretation of the plotted results.

code_label: Financial crash prediction as benchmark problem
text_span: A crucial problem in the ﬁnancial industry is to pre- dict how networks react to perturbations caused, for example, by a rapid drop of the market value of an in- stitution [37, 38].
rationale: Introduces the finance application motivating the benchmark.

code_label: Financial equilibrium encoded as cost function minimum
text_span: The classical cost function F(v) := [v −˜C(1 −C)−1 [Dp −b(v, p)]]2 ≥0 depending on the market values v has its global min- imum at ﬁnancial equilibrium
rationale: Describes the optimization objective used to build the Hamiltonian.

code_label: Binary encoding of market values
text_span: The market values vi are now encoded in classical bits, which are then promoted to qubits
rationale: States the discretization and qubit encoding step.

code_label: Truncated Legendre expansion makes polynomial Hamiltonian
text_span: If the expansion is truncated at level r, the failure functions bi(vi, p) are only polynomials of degree r in vi.
rationale: Explains how the nonlinearity is converted into a polynomial form.

code_label: Financial benchmark instance choices
text_span: We benchmark ﬁnancial networks consisting of n ∈{3, 4} institutions and m = 7 assets.
rationale: Specifies the benchmark instance sizes.

code_label: Resource explosion in financial Hamiltonian
text_span: a problem with n = 3, q = 5, and r = 3 al- ready introduces ntot terms = 1968 terms.
rationale: Quantifies the scale of the generated Hamiltonian.

code_label: Term truncation and thresholding as resource controls
text_span: This gives rise to the opportunity to save resources by only con- sidering the terms with the dominating coeﬃcients.
rationale: Describes a practical simplification strategy.

code_label: Parity outperforms standard implementation for financial crash benchmark
text_span: Especially when taking many terms into ac- count (which is equivalent to using a low chopping threshold), the parity embedding clearly outperforms the standard implementation when considering the number of CNOT gates as the ﬁgure of merit.
rationale: States the main benchmark outcome for the finance case.

code_label: Native 4-body couplers improve parity further
text_span: With that strategy, the advantage of the parity architecture is even more prominent.
rationale: Reports the effect of using 4-body couplers.

code_label: Electronic structure ground state as benchmark
text_span: Finding the ground state of molecules is a fundamen- tal challenge in contemporary molecular physics and quantum chemistry.
rationale: Introduces the chemistry benchmark motivation.

code_label: Mapping to sigma-z terms via Hilbert-space replication
text_span: They perform a mapping from a Hamiltonian containing arbitrary Pauli matrices to σz-interactions only, by replicating the n-qubit Hilbert space r times
locator: 4.4.2 Mapping the Electronic Structure Hamiltonian to σz-terms
rationale: Describes the transformation used before parity compilation.

code_label: Approximation improves with replication factor
text_span: With increasing r, more quantum eﬀects are taken into account and the approximation error drops.
locator: 4.4.2 Mapping the Electronic Structure Hamiltonian to σz-terms
rationale: States the tradeoff between resources and accuracy.

code_label: Electronic structure Hamiltonian can become exponentially large
text_span: H′ can include an expo- nential number of terms, resulting in an exponential number of qubits in the parity mapping.
locator: 4.4.2 Mapping the Electronic Structure Hamiltonian to σz-terms
rationale: Identifies a scalability limitation of the approach.

code_label: Reduced active orbitals for LiH due to resource limits
text_span: Due to limitations in com- putational resources, we therefore only consider three orbitals as active in the LiH molecule
rationale: Explicitly states a resource-based restriction.

code_label: Parity threshold depends on molecule and replication factor
text_span: It is obvious that a threshold for the par- ity mapping to consume fewer CNOT gates exists at r = 5 for H2, while for LiH this threshold is already at r = 2
rationale: Reports molecule-specific crossover points.

code_label: 4-body couplers always favor parity in chemistry benchmarks
text_span: For the implementation with constraint gates, the gate ratio is always signiﬁcantly below 1.
rationale: Summarizes the strongest parity advantage in the chemistry case.

code_label: No ancilla qubits considered
text_span: no ancilla qubits (which might be necessary for compilation and would introduce additional constraints and therefore CNOT gates) were considered.
rationale: States an omitted factor that could affect resource counts.

code_label: Parity advantage grows with larger replication factor
text_span: the parity architecture clearly outperforms the direct embedding of interactions in terms of CNOT gates, especially for large values of r.
rationale: Summarizes the chemistry benchmark trend.

code_label: Parity architecture promising beyond NISQ-era
text_span: the parity architecture is a promising candidate for developing scalable quantum optimization devices beyond the NISQ-era.
rationale: Concluding forward-looking assessment.
